nodes.title: Cache
nodes.description: Keep a copy of frequently accessed data somewhere fast so you avoid repeating expensive fetches or computations.

nodes.title: Cache Hit and Miss
nodes.description: A cache hit means the data you need is already stored nearby; a cache miss means it is not, so the system must fetch it from the slower original source.

nodes.title: IP Addressing
nodes.description: Every device on a network gets a unique numerical address so that data knows where to be sent and received.

nodes.title: TCP vs UDP
nodes.description: TCP and UDP are the two main protocols that control how data is broken into packets and delivered, with TCP guaranteeing delivery and UDP prioritizing speed.

nodes.title: Cache-Aside Pattern
nodes.description: The application checks the cache first, and on a miss it fetches from the database and writes the result back into the cache itself before returning it.

nodes.title: Cache Eviction Policies
nodes.description: When a cache is full, a policy such as Least Recently Used or Least Frequently Used decides which existing entries to drop to make room for new ones.

nodes.title: Cache Invalidation
nodes.description: Removing or updating stale entries in a cache so callers never read outdated data after the underlying source changes.

nodes.title: DNS
nodes.description: DNS is a global directory that translates human-readable domain names like google.com into the numerical IP addresses computers use to connect.

nodes.title: HTTP
nodes.description: HTTP is the request-and-response protocol that browsers and servers use to exchange web pages and data over the internet.

nodes.title: REST APIs
nodes.description: A REST API is a standardized way for programs to communicate over HTTP using plain URLs and verbs like GET, POST, and DELETE.

nodes.title: Subnetting
nodes.description: Subnetting divides a large network into smaller logical groups so that traffic stays organized and security boundaries are easier to enforce.

nodes.title: Time-to-Live (TTL)
nodes.description: Attach an expiry duration to each cached entry so it is automatically discarded after a set number of seconds, preventing data from going stale indefinitely.

nodes.title: Cache Stampede
nodes.description: When a popular cached entry expires, many concurrent requests all miss at once and simultaneously hit the database before the cache is repopulated, briefly overwhelming the system.

nodes.title: CDN
nodes.description: A CDN caches copies of your static files on servers around the world so users fetch content from a nearby node rather than a single distant origin server.

nodes.title: Load Balancing
nodes.description: A load balancer spreads incoming requests across multiple servers so no single machine is overwhelmed and the service stays fast and available.

nodes.title: TLS and HTTPS
nodes.description: TLS encrypts data in transit between a client and server so that anyone eavesdropping on the network cannot read or alter it.

nodes.title: WebSockets
nodes.description: WebSockets keep a persistent, two-way connection open between a client and server so data can stream in both directions without re-connecting for each message.

nodes.title: Write-Through Cache
nodes.description: Every write goes to the cache and the underlying data store at the same time, keeping them always in sync at the cost of slightly slower individual writes.

nodes.title: Distributed Cache
nodes.description: A cache layer spread across multiple machines (such as Redis Cluster) so no single node's memory limit or failure can take down the entire caching tier.

nodes.title: HTTP/2
nodes.description: HTTP/2 is an upgrade to HTTP that multiplexes multiple requests over one connection simultaneously, cutting the overhead that slows down modern web pages.
